key_findings.title: Bias is a Math Problem, AI Bias is a Technical Problem: 10-year Literature Review of AI/LLM Bias Research Reveals Narrow [Gender-Centric] Conceptions of 'Bias', and Academia-Industry Gap
key_findings.summary: A systematic review of 189 papers from ACL, FAccT, NeurIPS, and AAAI shows that most AI/LLM bias work lacks explicit definitions of bias, focuses heavily on gender (82%), and rarely provides deployment recommendations, highlighting a gap between academic findings and industry practice.

key_findings.title: Pushing the Limits of LLMs in Quantum Operations
key_findings.summary: Benchmarks four publicly available LLMs (WolframLLM, ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek) on generating quantum gate designs; Gemini is fastest, and all models produce usable quantum code ~80% of the time, indicating LLMs can become rapid collaborators for quantum computing workflows.

key_findings.title: Conversational Agents and the Understanding of Human Language: Reflections on AI, LLMs, and Cognitive Science
key_findings.summary: Analyzes the relationship between NLP progress and cognitive science, concluding that despite impressive performance of modern LLMs, they have not substantially advanced scientific understanding of human language processing.

key_findings.title: Behavioral Economics of AI: LLM Biases and Corrections
key_findings.summary: Extensive experiments reveal that larger, more advanced LLMs exhibit more human‑like decision patterns in preference tasks, while in belief‑based tasks they often produce rational responses; prompting strategies can further reduce systematic biases.

key_findings.title: Who Controls the Conversation? User Perspectives On Generative AI (LLM) System Prompts
key_findings.summary: Explores user attitudes toward hidden system prompts that steer LLM behavior; users desire transparency, value‑aligned prompts, and more control, suggesting design guidelines for governance of LLM deployments.

key_findings.title: How K-12 Educators Use AI: LLM-Assisted Qualitative Analysis at Scale
key_findings.summary: Introduces a reproducible pipeline that leverages LLMs to conduct large‑scale qualitative analysis of 13,000+ educator‑AI interactions, uncovering patterns in prompt strategies, adaptation, and evaluation of AI‑generated instructional content.

key_findings.title: AIS-LLM: A Unified Framework for Maritime Trajectory Prediction, Anomaly Detection, and Collision Risk Assessment with Explainable Forecasting
key_findings.summary: Presents a multimodal architecture that combines time‑series AIS data with a large language model to jointly perform trajectory prediction, anomaly detection, and collision risk assessment, outperforming task‑specific baselines and offering explainable situation summaries.

synthesis:
The literature from 2024‑2026 shows the field of AI LLMs moving beyond pure language modeling toward domain‑specific integration, governance, and societal impact. Recent surveys of bias research reveal a persistent narrow focus (mainly gender) and a lack of operational guidance, underscoring the need for broader fairness definitions and stronger academia‑industry pathways. Benchmarking studies such as the quantum‑operations paper demonstrate that LLMs are becoming practical co‑developers across highly technical domains, with performance differences now measured not only by accuracy but also by generation speed and code reliability.

Parallel work interrogates the epistemic limits of LLMs. The cognitive‑science reflection argues that despite scaling, LLMs still do not illuminate human language mechanisms, a point echoed by behavioral‑economics experiments that find LLMs mimic human biases in preference tasks while behaving more rationally in belief‑based contexts. Prompt engineering emerges as a critical lever: user‑centered studies on system prompts reveal demand for transparency and controllability, informing policy proposals for prompt disclosure and value alignment.

Application‑focused research highlights the versatility of LLMs. In education, novel pipelines enable large‑scale qualitative analysis of teacher‑AI dialogues, offering actionable insights for instructional design. In maritime traffic management, multimodal AIS‑LLM systems illustrate how LLMs can fuse structured sensor data with natural‑language reasoning to deliver unified prediction, anomaly detection, and risk assessment with explainable outputs.

Overall, the trajectory points to three converging trends: (1) **Cross‑modal integration**—LLMs are being embedded with non‑textual data streams (time‑series, code, sensor feeds) to solve domain‑specific problems; (2) **Governance and transparency**—system prompts, bias definitions, and deployment guidelines are increasingly recognized as essential for trustworthy AI; and (3) **Human‑LLM alignment**—research is moving toward methods that harness LLMs' human‑like decision patterns while correcting systematic biases through prompting and fine‑tuning. These developments, together with foundational works such as BERT (2018) and GPT‑4 (2023), set the stage for the next generation of LLMs that are not only larger but also more controllable, multimodal, and socially responsible.
